title: Stress Signals: p38 and JNK, p53, Unfolded Proteins and Oxidants

generated.pipeline: extract → Gemini draft → Claude Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In unstressed cells, about half of any newly synthesized batch of p53 is destroyed within about {{c1::twenty minutes}}.
cards.quote: Your cells build p53 all day and destroy half of any new batch within about twenty minutes.

cards.front: Why do cells continuously synthesize and rapidly degrade stress responders like p53 instead of transcribing them only when danger arrives?
cards.back: Lifting a restraint lets pre-made responder accumulate immediately, avoiding the delay of reading a gene and building a new protein during danger.
cards.why: Many stress pathways hold responders back—either by constant destruction or by a binding partner—so stress only has to release the brake.
cards.quote: if the responder already exists and is held back, the cell only has to let go.

cards.front: Under constant synthesis and first-order destruction, a responder's steady-state level equals synthesis rate divided by the {{c1::destruction rate constant}}.
cards.quote: Under constant synthesis and first-order destruction, a responder's steady-state pool obeys: steady-state level = synthesis rate ÷ destruction rate constant
cards.section: Built to turn on fast: p53–MDM2 and Keap1–Nrf2

cards.front: For first-order protein destruction with rate constant k_d, the responder's half-life equals {{c1::ln 2 ÷ k_d}}.
cards.quote: Because half-life varies inversely with that constant (half-life = ln 2 ÷ k_d), lengthening half-life raises steady state by the same factor with no new transcription.
cards.section: Built to turn on fast: p53–MDM2 and Keap1–Nrf2

cards.front: Under constant synthesis and first-order destruction, how does lengthening a stress responder's half-life change its steady-state pool without any new transcription?
cards.back: It raises the steady-state pool by the exact same factor.
cards.why: Steady state equals synthesis rate divided by k_d, and half-life is inversely proportional to k_d, so slowing destruction multiplies half-life and steady state equally.
cards.quote: lengthening half-life raises steady state by the same factor with no new transcription.
cards.section: Built to turn on fast: p53–MDM2 and Keap1–Nrf2

cards.front: A stress responder is made at a constant 80 units per hour and destroyed with first-order rate constant k_d = 4 per hour. If stress slows destruction fivefold with no change in synthesis, what are the initial and new steady-state levels?
cards.back: Initial steady state = 80 ÷ 4 = 20 units. New k_d = 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 per hour, so new steady state = 80 ÷ 0.8 = 100 units.
cards.why: Under constant synthesis and first-order destruction, steady-state level = synthesis rate ÷ k_d, so cutting k_d fivefold raises steady state fivefold without new transcription.
cards.quote: At 60 units per hour and a rate constant of 2 per hour (half-life ~21 min), steady state is 30 units
cards.section: Built to turn on fast: p53–MDM2 and Keap1–Nrf2

cards.front: A responder sits at a steady state of 50 units with a 20-minute half-life under constant synthesis and first-order destruction. If destruction suddenly stops completely while synthesis continues unchanged, roughly how long does it take to double to 100 units?
cards.back: About 29 minutes. Since k_d = ln 2 ÷ 20 min ≈ 0.0347 min⁻¹, synthesis rate = 50 × 0.0347 ≈ 1.73 units/min; adding 50 units takes 50 ÷ 1.73 = 20 ÷ ln 2 ≈ 28.9 minutes.
cards.why: Halting destruction lets ongoing synthesis double a protein with a ~20-minute half-life in under half an hour, with no new transcription required.
cards.quote: From p53's ~20-minute half-life, halting destruction lets steady synthesis double the pool in under half an hour.
cards.section: Built to turn on fast: p53–MDM2 and Keap1–Nrf2

cards.front: In unstressed cells, p53 is restrained by MDM2, an {{c1::E3 ubiquitin ligase}} that covers p53's gene-activating region and tags p53 for the proteasome.
cards.quote: MDM2, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that grips a short helix at p53's front end, covering its gene-activating region and tagging p53 with ubiquitin for the proteasome.
cards.section: DNA breaks: p53 and MDM2

cards.front: Why do p53 and MDM2 form a negative feedback loop?
cards.back: As a transcription factor, p53 switches on the MDM2 gene itself, ordering synthesis of the E3 ubiquitin ligase that marks p53 for destruction.
cards.quote: Crucially, p53 switches on the MDM2 gene itself—ordering its own destroyer in a negative feedback loop
cards.section: DNA breaks: p53 and MDM2

cards.front: How does a break across both DNA strands release p53 from MDM2 restraint?
cards.back: The break activates the kinase ATM; ATM and kinases beneath it phosphorylate both p53's MDM2-binding stretch and MDM2 itself, loosening their grip so destruction slows sharply.
cards.quote: ATM and the kinases beneath it phosphorylate both p53's MDM2-binding stretch and MDM2 itself, loosening their grip so destruction slows sharply.
cards.section: DNA breaks: p53 and MDM2

cards.front: What three classes of target genes does accumulated p53 activate after DNA damage?
cards.back: p21 (which blocks kinases driving cell division), DNA repair genes, and—under severe damage—cell-death genes.
cards.quote: Accumulated p53 activates p21 (blocking kinases that drive cell division), DNA repair genes, and—under severe damage—cell-death genes
cards.section: DNA breaks: p53 and MDM2

cards.front: A small molecule that plugs MDM2's p53-binding cleft is added to healthy cells with intact DNA. What happens to p53 levels over the next hour, and why?
cards.back: p53 climbs sharply even without DNA damage, because continuous p53 synthesis proceeds while MDM2 cannot grip p53 or tag it for proteasomal destruction.
cards.why: This is the mechanism of nutlin-3: blocking the restraint releases p53 accumulation without needing DNA breaks or ATM.
cards.quote: p53 climbs sharply without DNA damage: synthesis continues while MDM2 cannot grip or tag p53 for the proteasome
cards.section: DNA breaks: p53 and MDM2

cards.front: How do some tumors, such as sarcomas, keep the p53 pathway suppressed even though their TP53 gene is intact?
cards.back: They carry extra copies of the MDM2 gene, keeping excess MDM2 brake pressed down on p53.
cards.why: Cells lacking active p53 keep dividing with broken chromosomes, whether TP53 is mutated (mostly in its DNA-binding domain) or MDM2 is amplified.
cards.quote: Some tumors, sarcomas among them, keep p53 intact and carry extra copies of MDM2 instead, keeping the brake pressed down.
cards.section: DNA breaks: p53 and MDM2

cards.front: Tumor cells carrying a p53 DNA-binding mutation show far more p53 protein and much less MDM2 mRNA than neighboring normal cells; a proteasome inhibitor raises p53 strongly in normal cells but barely changes it in the tumor cells. What explains all three observations?
cards.back: Based on the p53–MDM2 negative feedback and proteasomal degradation rules, mutant p53 cannot bind DNA to activate MDM2 transcription; with little MDM2 made, mutant p53 is rarely degraded, so it accumulates and proteasome inhibition has little further effect.
cards.why: Most TP53 cancer mutations hit the DNA-binding domain, breaking both downstream protective gene induction and the self-limiting MDM2 feedback loop.
cards.quote: making TP53, the gene for p53, the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer, mostly in its DNA-binding domain.
cards.section: DNA breaks: p53 and MDM2

cards.front: In calm cells, the continuously made transcription factor Nrf2 is gripped by {{c1::Keap1}} (part of a ubiquitin ligase), keeping its half-life well under an hour.
cards.why: When activated, Nrf2 turns on protective enzyme genes, including enzymes that join electrophiles to glutathione for excretion.
cards.quote: Made constantly, Nrf2 is gripped by Keap1 (part of a ubiquitin ligase), keeping its half-life well under an hour in calm cells.
cards.section: Chemical threats: Keap1 and Nrf2

cards.front: How can Keap1 detect a broad family of structurally unrelated electrophiles rather than only one shaped ligand?
cards.back: Instead of using a shaped receptor pocket, Keap1 senses electron hunger directly through unusually reactive cysteine side chains whose sulfur atoms give up electrons easily.
cards.why: Electrophiles are molecules short of electrons; mouse Keap1 contains 25 cysteines among 624 amino acids, several unusually reactive.
cards.quote: Unlike a shaped receptor pocket, Keap1 reads hunger for electrons, sensing a broad family of unrelated chemicals.
cards.section: Chemical threats: Keap1 and Nrf2

cards.front: On the current model of Keap1–Nrf2 signaling, electrophile-modified Keap1 stops passing older Nrf2 on for destruction while still gripping it. If all new protein synthesis is blocked when an electrophile arrives, how much Nrf2 enters the nucleus, and why?
cards.back: Very little Nrf2 reaches the nucleus, because altered Keap1 continues gripping the older Nrf2; nuclear entry depends on newly synthesized Nrf2 escaping once Keap1 catchers are occupied.
cards.quote: Very little: because altered Keap1 still grips the older Nrf2, nuclear entry depends on newly made Nrf2 escaping once Keap1 is occupied.
cards.section: Chemical threats: Keap1 and Nrf2

cards.front: Mice whose Keap1 has serine replacing cysteine 151 restrain Nrf2 normally without treatment, yet sulforaphane barely activates Nrf2 in them while other electrophile inducers still work. What does this show?
cards.back: Which reactive cysteine responds on Keap1 depends on the electrophile: cysteine 151 is needed for sulforaphane sensing, not for basal Nrf2 restraint or for every inducer.
cards.quote: Which cysteine responds depends on the compound: in mice with serine replacing cysteine 151, sulforaphane does much less to Nrf2 while other inducers still work.
cards.section: Chemical threats: Keap1 and Nrf2

cards.front: After blocking all new protein synthesis with cycloheximide, a stress responder falls from 160 units to 20 units over 45 minutes in untreated cells, and from 320 units to 160 units over 45 minutes in electrophile-treated cells. What were the untreated and treated half-lives, and what does this show?
cards.back: Half-life rose from 15 minutes to 45 minutes, showing that the electrophile slowed destruction. Untreated: 160 → 80 → 40 → 20 is 3 halvings in 45 min (45 ÷ 3 = 15 min). Treated: 320 → 160 is 1 halving in 45 min (45 min).
cards.why: Stopping synthesis isolates first-order decay; a longer half-life directly reflects a lower destruction rate constant k_d.
cards.quote: On the current view, altered Keap1 stops passing Nrf2 on for destruction, so Keap1 catchers fill up and newly made Nrf2 enters the nucleus.
cards.section: Chemical threats: Keap1 and Nrf2

cards.front: In the three-tier stress MAPK cascades, the MAP2Ks above p38 are {{c1::MKK3 and MKK6}}, whereas MKK4 and MKK7 sit above JNK.
cards.why: Many distinct MAP3Ks sit above these MAP2Ks, wiring UV light, heat, sudden salt changes, oxidants, bacterial products, TNF, and interleukin-1 into p38 and JNK.
cards.quote: Above p38 sit the MAP2Ks MKK3 and MKK6, above JNK sit MKK4 and MKK7, and above those sit many MAP3Ks wired to distinct stresses.
cards.section: Three-tier stress relays: p38 and JNK

cards.front: In the standard MAPK route, switching on p38 and JNK—like ERK—requires a MAP2K to phosphorylate both a {{c1::threonine and a tyrosine}} one residue apart.
cards.quote: In the standard route, p38 and JNK—like ERK—require a MAP2K to phosphorylate both a threonine and a tyrosine one residue apart.
cards.section: Three-tier stress relays: p38 and JNK

cards.front: Thioredoxin normally binds and inhibits the MAP3K ASK1 until oxidants cause thioredoxin to let go. If a mutation stops thioredoxin from binding ASK1, what happens to p38 and JNK in an unstressed cell, and why?
cards.back: p38 and JNK would be expected to gain phosphates even without oxidants, because ASK1 is freed from partner restraint and switches on its downstream MAP2Ks constitutively.
cards.quote: Freed from thioredoxin, ASK1 would be expected to switch on its MAP2Ks without oxidants, so p38 and JNK would gain phosphates in an unstressed cell.
cards.section: Three-tier stress relays: p38 and JNK

cards.front: Suppose a cell is exposed to oxidants at the same moment all new protein synthesis is blocked. Contrast the effect of blocking synthesis on nuclear Nrf2 accumulation (on the current occupancy model) versus initial ASK1 activation, and explain why.
cards.back: Nuclear Nrf2 accumulation is largely prevented whereas initial ASK1 activation can still proceed. This rests on the two restraint rules: altered Keap1 still grips older Nrf2 so nuclear entry needs newly synthesized Nrf2, whereas intact ASK1 already waits ready until oxidants make thioredoxin let go.
cards.quote: One MAP3K, ASK1, repeats partner restraint: thioredoxin holds ASK1 off until oxidants make thioredoxin let go.
cards.section: Three-tier stress relays: p38 and JNK

cards.front: What are two major downstream jobs of p38 in immune and stressed cells?
cards.back: In immune cells p38 raises TNF and interleukin-1 output partly through MK2, and MK2 phosphorylates Hsp27, a small chaperone protecting stressed proteins.
cards.quote: in immune cells p38 raises TNF and interleukin-1 output partly through MK2, and MK2 phosphorylates Hsp27, a small chaperone protecting stressed proteins.
cards.section: Three-tier stress relays: p38 and JNK

cards.front: What are two main downstream effects of JNK activation?
cards.back: JNK phosphorylates serines 63 and 73 of c-Jun (an AP-1 partner) to strengthen gene activation, and persistent stress pushes JNK toward cell death.
cards.quote: phosphorylates serines 63 and 73 of c-Jun, the AP-1 partner from the previous lesson, strengthening gene activation. Persistent stress pushes JNK toward cell death
cards.section: Three-tier stress relays: p38 and JNK

cards.front: Cultured sensory neurons from mouse embryos lacking DLK resist both axon degeneration and cell death after losing nerve growth factor. What does this result indicate about DLK in neurons?
cards.back: DLK feeds the JNK stress cascade in neurons and drives axon degeneration and cell death when nerve growth factor is withdrawn.
cards.quote: cultured sensory neurons from mouse embryos lacking DLK resist both axon degeneration and cell death after losing nerve growth factor.
cards.section: Three-tier stress relays: p38 and JNK

cards.front: A blot made from millions of gamma-irradiated cells shows p53 rising once and slowly fading over a day. Why does this measurement say little about p53 dynamics in any single cell?
cards.back: Averaging many cells whose individual p53 pulses are out of step blurs discrete oscillations into a single smooth rise-and-fall curve.
cards.why: Like averaging a thousand out-of-step strobe lights into a steady glow, population averages erase asynchronous single-cell pulses.
cards.quote: The second film showed why dish blots blur single-cell pulses—like averaging a thousand out-of-step strobe lights into a steady glow.
cards.section: Pulses, not a dial: reading the timing of p53

cards.front: In single human cells after gamma irradiation, how does increasing the radiation dose affect p53 pulses?
cards.back: Individual pulses keep a fixed average height and width, while higher doses raise the average pulse count (even as genetically identical neighbors fire none, one, two, or more).
cards.quote: Individual cells fired discrete p53 pulses of fixed average height and width; higher doses raised the average pulse count, while genetically identical neighbours gave none, one, two or more.
cards.section: Pulses, not a dial: reading the timing of p53

cards.front: In single-cell movies with cyan-tagged p53 and yellow-tagged MDM2, does yellow MDM2 peak before, with, or slightly after cyan p53 during each pulse, and why?
cards.back: Slightly after cyan p53, because p53 must rise first to drive new MDM2 transcription and synthesis; after that lag, rising MDM2 knocks p53 back down.
cards.quote: Slightly after cyan p53: p53 must rise first to drive new MDM2 synthesis, and after that lag yellow MDM2 builds up and knocks cyan p53 down.
cards.section: Pulses, not a dial: reading the timing of p53

cards.front: How does the single-cell p53 response to ultraviolet light differ from the response to gamma rays?
cards.back: Gamma rays (double-strand breaks) elicit fixed-size pulses whose count increases with dose, whereas ultraviolet light produces one pulse whose height and length grow with dose.
cards.why: Signal level carries information alongside timing; in chemotherapy-treated cancer cells, death also depends on how high p53 climbs and how soon.
cards.quote: Fixed-size pulses belong to gamma rays (double-strand breaks). Ultraviolet light gives one pulse whose height and length grow with dose
cards.section: Pulses, not a dial: reading the timing of p53

cards.front: Researchers used timed doses of the MDM2 blocker nutlin-3 in a human cell line to hold p53 steady at the height of one natural pulse instead of letting it pulse. Pulsing cells tended to recover and divide, whereas steady cells more often entered senescence—even when total integrated p53 was matched. What did this experiment demonstrate?
cards.back: Signal shape itself carries cell-fate information: resting on the controlled comparison at equal peak height and equal total p53, sustained p53 activates senescence genes more strongly than pulsing p53.
cards.why: Matching both peak level and total p53 ruled out simple concentration or cumulative-dose explanations, isolating temporal dynamics as causal in that cell line.
cards.quote: Holding p53 up also meant more p53 in total, but at equal total p53, sustained p53 still switched on senescence genes more strongly: signal shape mattered.
cards.section: Pulses, not a dial: reading the timing of p53

cards.front: In a two-protein circuit where activator A induces its own destroyer D, what features make A pulse repeatedly instead of settling flat, and how can DNA damage control the number of pulses?
cards.back: By the delayed negative-feedback rule, enough synthesis delay plus a steep response lets A overshoot before arriving D knocks it down, after which D decays and A rises again; gating D's grip with a damage kinase keeps pulsing only while DNA breaks remain.
cards.quote: With enough delay and a steep response, negative feedback oscillates: making D takes time so A overshoots, arriving D knocks A down
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Suppose a pulsing activator drives both a short-lived arrest-and-repair protein and a long-lived permanent-arrest protein. Predict how one pulse versus many repeated pulses steers cell fate, and explain why.
cards.back: One pulse produces temporary arrest and repair, whereas many pulses trigger permanent exit from division. Resting on the pulse-counting rule, the short-lived target rises and falls with each pulse while the long-lived target accumulates across pulses until crossing threshold.
cards.quote: a long-lived permanent-arrest target that accumulates bit by bit across pulses until many pulses push it over threshold.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: On the leading accounts, how do the three ER-membrane sensors (IRE1, PERK, and ATF6) detect a backlog of unfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum?
cards.back: The ER chaperone BiP holds the sensors quiet until unfolded protein chains pull BiP away, and unfolded chains also bind IRE1 directly.
cards.quote: On the leading accounts, BiP holds them quiet until unfolded chains pull BiP away, and unfolded chains also bind IRE1 directly.
cards.section: Three sensors in the folding compartment: the unfolded protein response

cards.front: Once clustered by ER stress, IRE1 activates a cytoplasmic RNase that cuts a segment out of {{c1::XBP1}} mRNA in animals (or HAC1 in yeast) before a ligase rejoins the ends.
cards.why: Only the spliced mRNA yields an active transcription factor that switches on ER chaperone genes.
cards.quote: Clustering switches on IRE1's cytoplasmic RNase, which cuts a segment out of one mRNA—HAC1 in yeast, XBP1 in animals—before a ligase rejoins the ends
cards.section: Three sensors in the folding compartment: the unfolded protein response

cards.front: In mammalian XBP1 mRNA, IRE1 removes 26 nucleotides before ligation. Why does this alter the protein's entire downstream tail instead of simply deleting eight or nine amino acids?
cards.back: It shifts the reading frame downstream, creating a new tail that turns the protein into an active transcription factor, because codons are read in threes and 26 leaves a remainder of 2.
cards.quote: Codons are read in threes, and 26 is not a multiple of three (remainder 2). Removing 26 nucleotides shifts the reading frame
cards.section: Three sensors in the folding compartment: the unfolded protein response

cards.front: During ER folding stress, PERK phosphorylates the ribosome initiation factor {{c1::eIF2α}}, slowing global protein synthesis so fewer new chains enter the ER.
cards.quote: PERK phosphorylates eIF2α, a ribosome initiation factor, slowing global protein synthesis so fewer new chains enter the ER.
cards.section: Three sensors in the folding compartment: the unfolded protein response

cards.front: How does ATF6 switch on ER chaperone genes during the unfolded protein response?
cards.back: Like Notch, stressed ATF6 moves from the ER to the Golgi, where proteases cleave off a fragment that enters the nucleus to activate chaperone genes.
cards.quote: Like Notch, stressed ATF6 moves to the Golgi, where proteases release a fragment that enters the nucleus to activate chaperone genes.
cards.section: Three sensors in the folding compartment: the unfolded protein response

cards.front: If a drug prevents membrane proteins from moving out of the ER to the Golgi during ER folding stress, which of the three UPR sensors (IRE1, PERK, or ATF6) is directly blocked from signaling, and why?
cards.back: ATF6 is directly blocked, because ATF6 must travel to the Golgi for proteases to release its nuclear fragment, whereas IRE1 and PERK act directly from the ER membrane on cytoplasmic substrates.
cards.quote: Like Notch, stressed ATF6 moves to the Golgi, where proteases release a fragment that enters the nucleus to activate chaperone genes.
cards.section: Three sensors in the folding compartment: the unfolded protein response

cards.front: When treated with a drug causing ER protein misfolding, normal cells phosphorylate eIF2α and sharply slow amino-acid incorporation into new protein; PERK-deficient cells show neither change and die at lower drug doses. What does this show about PERK's initial effect?
cards.back: PERK's early effect is protective: phosphorylating eIF2α cuts global translation and reduces the load of new polypeptide chains entering the stressed ER.
cards.quote: PERK phosphorylates eIF2α, a ribosome initiation factor, slowing global protein synthesis so fewer new chains enter the ER.
cards.section: Three sensors in the folding compartment: the unfolded protein response

cards.front: If an ER folding backlog persists rather than resolving, how do the PERK and IRE1 branches shift the response toward cell death?
cards.back: PERK's branch switches on the death-promoting transcription factor CHOP, and IRE1 recruits an adaptor that feeds ASK1 and JNK.
cards.why: Brief stress mainly calls for repair across all three branches, whereas prolonged or severe stress signals that repair is failing, though adaptive and death signals can overlap.
cards.quote: If the backlog lasts, PERK's branch switches on CHOP, a death-promoting transcription factor, and IRE1 recruits an adaptor feeding ASK1 and JNK.
cards.section: Three sensors in the folding compartment: the unfolded protein response

cards.front: Why do children and mice born without functional PERK develop diabetes early in life?
cards.back: Heavy secretors depend on PERK: children born without it develop diabetes within months of birth, and in mice the diabetes comes with too few insulin-producing pancreatic cells.
cards.why: Secreted proteins such as insulin fold inside the ER, making insulin-secreting cells unusually vulnerable when the UPR cannot throttle translation.
cards.quote: children born without working PERK develop diabetes within months of birth, and mice lacking PERK develop diabetes with too few insulin-producing pancreatic cells.
cards.section: Three sensors in the folding compartment: the unfolded protein response

cards.front: Suppose a cell lacks the MAP3K ASK1. Predict how this loss affects both its acute oxidant response and its response to a prolonged ER folding backlog, and explain why.
cards.back: Both signaling routes are blunted: under oxidants, releasing thioredoxin cannot activate ASK1 to drive p38 and JNK; under prolonged ER stress, IRE1's adaptor loses its ASK1 route to JNK (though PERK can still induce CHOP). This combines the thioredoxin–ASK1 restraint rule with IRE1's persistent-backlog pathway.
cards.quote: If the backlog lasts, PERK's branch switches on CHOP, a death-promoting transcription factor, and IRE1 recruits an adaptor feeding ASK1 and JNK.
cards.section: Three sensors in the folding compartment: the unfolded protein response

cards.front: How does the endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response combine both release of restraint and signal timing to steer cell fate?
cards.back: By the release-of-restraint rule, unfolded chains pull BiP off IRE1, PERK, and ATF6 (and bind IRE1 directly) to launch immediate repair; by the timing rule, brief stress favors repair whereas a persistent backlog adds death pathways (CHOP via PERK and ASK1–JNK via IRE1), alongside stress strength and cell state.
cards.quote: lifting a restraint starts the alarm, and backlog duration helps steer repair toward death.
cards.section: Three sensors in the folding compartment: the unfolded protein response
